title: Ten Wrestlers Entered. Ten Won Medals. India's Women Swept the U17 Asian Championships Without Dropping a Single Athlete.
excerpt: At the U17 Asian Wrestling Championships in Da Nang, India achieved a 100 per cent podium finish with two gold, three silver, and five bronze. Days earlier, the U23 men's freestyle team won the championship outright.
body:
Ten wrestlers entered. Ten reached the podium. India's women did not drop a single athlete from the medal count at the U17 Asian Wrestling Championships in Da Nang, Vietnam — a 100 per cent podium finish that announced the depth of the country's age-group pipeline with unmistakable clarity.

The final tally: two gold, three silver, and five bronze medals across all ten weight categories. And this came days after the Indian men's freestyle wrestling team was crowned undisputed champions at the U23 Asian Wrestling Championships in the same city, topping the medal table with 11 gold, seven silver, and nine bronze — 27 medals in total, ahead of traditional powerhouses Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan.

The Gold Standard

Diksha, competing in the 43kg category, was the standout performer of the U17 tournament. She cruised past opponents from Kyrgyzstan (8-0) and Vietnam (10-0) before delivering a commanding 6-0 shutout of Kyrgyzstan's Asangaryeva in the final. Not a single point conceded in the gold-medal bout.

In the 73kg class, Garima produced an attacking display that overwhelmed Mongolia's Namuuntsetseg Batbold 18-6. The scoreline tells the story — Garima was relentless, racking up points with a combination of throws and technical superiority that the Mongolian had no answer for.

Silver and Bronze

Nikita (49kg) and Antra (65kg) each claimed silver, both falling to Chinese opponents in the final — Nikita losing 2-10 to Yuan Yuting, and Antra going down 0-5 to Siyu Wei after an impressive semifinal win over Japan. Taniya (69kg) added a third silver, finishing runner-up after a hard-fought bout against Khadisha Flyuk.

The five bronze medals came through Palak (40kg), Anamika (46kg), Akshra (53kg), Sakshi (57kg), and Manya (61kg). Sakshi's bronze was particularly notable — she bounced back from a narrow semifinal loss to dismantle Kazakhstan's Arina Kuanyshova 10-0 in the medal playoff.

A System Producing Champions at Every Level

The Da Nang results are not an outlier. They are the latest evidence of a wrestling ecosystem that is now producing medal-worthy athletes from under-17 through to the senior level. The U23 men's freestyle team championship — India's first at that level — suggests the pipeline is not just wide but deep.

For the diaspora, Indian wrestling carries a particular resonance. The sport's heartland in Haryana and Punjab overlaps significantly with communities that have emigrated to North America, the UK, and Australia. When the World Wrestling Championships open in September 2026, the senior women's team — led by Asian Games squad members Antim Panghal, Nisha Dahiya, and Manisha Bhanwala — will carry the weight of these age-group results as evidence that the next generation is ready to push them.

The Bigger Picture

India's Asian Games wrestling squad for Aichi-Nagoya was finalised through selection trials in late May. World No. 1 Aman Sehrawat and the returning Bajrang Punia at 97kg headline the men's entries. The women's squad includes Panghal, who has been dominant at 53kg for two consecutive seasons.

The selection trials themselves generated headlines — Vinesh Phogat, the three-time Olympian, alleged the women's 53kg trials were not conducted fairly after her semifinal loss at the Indira Gandhi Stadium on May 30. The Wrestling Federation of India has not issued a formal response. Whether or not the controversy gains traction, the trials underscored the brutal internal competition that exists within Indian wrestling. When the talent pool is this deep, selection itself becomes the hardest fight.

The U17 results in Da Nang tell a quieter story, one that rarely makes headlines in mainstream Indian media. But ten medals from ten entries is a statistical anomaly that demands attention. These teenagers are not just competing at the Asian level — they are dominating it. The question is no longer whether India can produce wrestlers. It is whether the system can sustain this production line through to the Olympics and the World Championships.

Da Nang suggests the answer is yes.

Sources: Wrestling Federation of India, IANS, ANI, LatestLY
author: Diaspora Desk
